text: Children will engage with materials. <break time="0.8s" /> More purposefully, and for longer. <break time="0.8s" /> When there is some ambiguity involved. <break time="0.8s" /> And thus, something they are interested in figuring out. <break time="0.8s" /> In studies of toddlers and preschoolers. <break time="0.8s" /> Researchers have found. <break time="0.8s" /> That children spontaneously engage in more exploratory play. <break time="0.8s" /> And use more strategies for testing evidence. <break time="0.8s" /> With a toy designed to be difficult to figure out. <break time="0.8s" /> In one study. <break time="0.8s" /> Young children explored a lightbox. <break time="0.8s" /> That appeared to turn on and off. <break time="0.8s" /> When different blocks were placed on it. <break time="0.8s" /> In one condition. <break time="0.8s" /> The same block always turned the box on or off. <break time="0.8s" /> In another. <break time="0.8s" /> Inconsistent results were included. <break time="0.8s" /> For example. <break time="0.8s" /> A block that had previously turned the box on did not the next time. <break time="0.8s" /> When faced with inconsistent and difficult to interpret results. <break time="0.8s" /> Children spent more time exploring the lightbox. <break time="0.8s" /> And were more likely to provide causal explanations. <break time="0.8s" /> Trying to understand. <break time="0.8s" /> Why the objects did and did not turn on the lightbox. <break time="0.8s" /> Further researchers found. <break time="0.8s" /> That when children proposed causal explanations. <break time="0.8s" /> They tried out more strategies. <break time="0.8s" /> For testing their ideas.
